judge.reason: A flatly says "Nothing is wrong with you" with no medical history, which fails the must-pass facts check, while B hedges that and lists fuller warning signs, even though it is too long and uses bold bullet labels for a short chat reply to a teenager.

B opens with the answer, names going too fast as the common mistake, and gives one concrete interval plan in short prose with no bold labels or recap, while A is long, bullet-heavy with bold labels, and ends by repeating its own reassurance.

B keeps the skater off-center, uses one named light source, hides hands and face, and leaves the title for real type, while A asks the image model to render text, never says where the skater sits, doesn't name a light source, and names no hand finishing pass.

A names one light source, places the subject off-center, hides the hands and face, keeps all text out of the image, and sets the title afterward in a real font. B asks the model to render "CALÇADA" and "24 pages", names no light, gives no subject position, and has no hand finishing pass.

B puts the skater off-center, keeps the title and all text out of the render and names a real-font finishing pass, while A asks the image model to render text, leaves the skater's position unspecified and names no hand pass.

A prints a clear error for a missing file and counts only lines that start with an IPv4 address, while B crashes with a traceback on a missing file, counts non-IP tokens like 'foo' as addresses, and leaves an unused `ip_pattern = None`.
A exits with a clear 'cannot read' message on a missing file and checks argv, while B crashes with a raw FileNotFoundError traceback, has no argv check, and leaves an unused `IP_RE = None`.
A prints a clear 'error: cannot read ...' message and exits 1 on a missing file, while B crashes with a raw FileNotFoundError traceback.

A keeps to the supplied facts, shows its arithmetic and lists its unknowns, while B adds a margin of error that assumes a random sample the brief never gave and asserts a class-conflict effect and an afternoon-schedule concern that the supplied facts do not support.

A cites only the supplied facts as the user's own, opens with the recommendation, and states what is unknown. B names sources the brief never gave (a class timetable, a facilities dataset), asserts a benefit the facts don't support, and opens with a question rather than the finding.

B opens with the recommendation, shows its arithmetic, rounds the counts and cites the supplied facts as the user's own, while A opens with background, gives an exact-looking 'about 238' with no arithmetic, and invents 'facilities data' and 'timetable data' as sources.

A invents facts that were not in the brief (an early-applicant advantage, volunteers on hand, 'bring your gloves') and pads with filler and a summary ending, while B stays within the supplied facts and flags the missing sign-up detail with a placeholder instead of making one up.

B opens with the facts and has no stock phrases, while A opens with 'Exciting news for our community!', uses stock phrases ('right in the heart of', 'We can't wait to welcome you'), and has two habitual triads in 150 words.

A keeps to the supplied facts and flags the missing sign-up detail with a placeholder, while B invents 'vegetables, herbs, and flowers', a 'community bulletin board' and 'expected to fill quickly', and it leans on stock phrases like 'green thumbs' and 'eager to dig in'.

B is the stronger scene, with sharper dialogue, an escalation and a concrete pending ending, but it fails the must-pass fidelity check (339 words against a 300 ask, and it never shows three of eight machines out of order), while A passes fidelity but has a personified-light opener, a flat shape and a mood-image ending.

A has conflict, an escalating surveyor thread and sharp dialogue, and it is within length at 288 words. Its "Aye. Right." ending is weak but still leaves it open. B stays flat at one pitch, has little conflict, leans on weather and personification, and ends on mood with the clock ticking.

A runs 340 words against a 300-word ask, over the 10% limit, and its narration spells out the dilemma that the scene already shows. B stays at about 318 words, keeps every brief fact, and ends with the telling still open.

A has a numeric test plan with thresholds, a cleanup check and a low-graphics frame-time limit, and it says it was not run, while B has no frame-time or cleanup check, no sound or shake feedback, and no one-at-a-time tuning plan.

B's test plan has numeric thresholds, a frame-time check on the lowest setting, and a cleanup check, and it says nothing was run, while A has no performance or cleanup check, no stated core verb, and only a thin telegraph for feedback.

B's test plan has numeric thresholds, a lowest-settings frame-time check, a cleanup count and an explicit 'not run' statement, and its design layers several feedback channels, while A has no cleanup check, no lowest-quality test, and only flash and aim-line feedback.

A keeps to the supplied facts, uses placeholders for the gaps, and follows the dated goal/tried/changed/result/next shape with a wiring table. B states an unsupplied fact ("I wrote and uploaded the code"), keeps wiring only in prose, and ends with no next step.

A follows the goal/tried/changed/result/next shape, puts the wiring in a table and leaves placeholders for missing facts, while B is a prose narrative with no wiring table and no next step (failing B5, B6 and B7).

B keeps to the supplied facts, uses a wiring table, follows the goal/tried/result/changed/next shape and leaves placeholders for gaps, while A has wiring only in prose, no next step, and adds an unsupplied cause explanation about floating data lines.

A keeps every fact and adds a good and bad opening example, reasoned avoid-list entries and a request for three different scripts, while B has no example, gives no reasons for its avoids, makes a one-shot request and leans on a filler role line.

Both prompts keep all six facts, but B gives a committed voice, asks for a voice sample with [need:], explains why each stock phrase should be avoided and asks for three varied openings. A leans on an empty role line and adjectives, gives no example, and gives no reason for its avoid list.

A works at both widths, has a visible focus ring and a clear tape-measure and price-board direction, but fails on invented claims ('done while you wait on the bench', 'Fixed prices for the two most common jobs'); B has the same kind of invented claims ('Hems for trousers, skirts', 'done with care'), plus cramped hours text at 375px, only an underline on focus (no ring), a single serif face, and cards nested inside cards. I did not run the scanner script, so U8 is not counted for either file.
judge.note: Scores are out of 7 applicable checks (U8 excluded).

judge.reason: A uses only the supplied facts and has a distinct price-board look with visible focus styles, while B adds an unsupplied claim ('Careful alterations and repairs') and is a generic single-serif page with a card grid.

Both render cleanly at phone and desktop widths, but A has a clear price-board direction, two type faces and tokens, while B is a generic single-serif cream page; A still needs fixing because it adds unsupplied claims ('priced per garment', 'we will tell you what it needs', 'we will answer') that fail U6. I did not run the UI scanner, so U8 is excluded from both scores.

Both add details Sam never supplied, so both fail fidelity, but A adds more ("I miss being in goal", a training trial, coming early or staying late) and turns a one-match request into a move "from midfield to goalkeeper", and it ends on a pleasantry. B's additions are fewer (a Friday deadline, "not asking to swap full time", "confident") and it ends on a next step.

A invents commitments not in the brief (staying after training for distribution and positioning, a keeper possibly already picked), asserts 'I can handle pressure' and closes on a pleasantry, while B keeps to the supplied facts, in plain short lines, and ends on a concrete request.
